claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is controlled by the evolution of interfacial chemical short-range order.
Sustained mechanical loading progressively degrades or destroys interfacial short-range order.
Strong short-range order impedes dislocation nucleation and glide.
Loss of short-range order reduces local barriers to dislocation nucleation and motion.
Short-range-order degradation causes a transition from diffusion-dominated creep to dislocation-dominated plastic flow.
Slip and potentially twinning contribute to the later dislocation-dominated deformation regime.
The starting coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The starting multilayer has a well-defined nominal distribution of local short-range order.
Chemical complexity in high-entropy alloys can produce local stoichiometric deviations and chemical short-range order.
Severe, heterogeneous lattice distortion is characteristic of the proposed high-entropy-alloy multilayer.
Local chemical ordering and lattice distortion are reciprocally coupled.
Controlled pre-annealing enhances short-range order, whereas rapid quenching intentionally disrupts it.
Multilayers with higher initial short-range order will have a delayed onset of plastic flow.
Multilayers with higher initial short-range order will have lower creep strain rates than specimens with disrupted short-range order.
Continued loading will produce increasingly homogeneous plastic flow as initially resistant regions succumb.
The progression of plastic deformation will correlate with a measurable localized loss of short-range order.
Interface chemistry and lattice distortion dominate deformation behavior within the stated stress and temperature window.
The proposed mechanism is limited to conditions that preserve the nanoscale multilayer and avoid bulk phase transformation or catastrophic failure.

If enhanced- and disrupted-SRO specimens show no statistically significant differences in creep rate, dislocation activity, and softening under identical loading, the proposed SRO-control hypothesis is falsified.
